_why: Which model to run, by how much VRAM you have. Separate from engines.json on purpose: that file holds PROVIDER facts (how to talk to a server), this one holds MODEL judgement (which weights to load). A provider row is config; a model row is a claim about quality, and a claim needs evidence.
_status_rule: Every entry is `measured` or `available`, and the distinction is the point. `measured` means it ran the 40-key stress corpus through this tool and the numbers below are its own. `available` means the GGUF exists and the family looks promising — nothing more. A larger sibling of a winner is a CANDIDATE, never a recommendation: TranslateGemma proved it, where the 12B was flawless and the 4B lost a brand name and dropped a key. Promote a row by running it, not by reasoning about it.
_size_does_not_predict_fit: Measured on an 8 GB card 2026-07-27: gemma3:12b and translategemma:12b are BOTH 8.1 GB on disk, and took 227 s and 1,145 s respectively for the same 40 keys — 5x apart. Disk size tells you almost nothing about whether a model is usable on your card; architecture, context and offload behaviour decide it. So the tiers below are grouped by what was MEASURED to work, not by arithmetic on file sizes.
_the_corpus: 40 keys chosen to break things: all 8 plural-pipe forms, 20 interpolations, 10 long paragraphs with named slots, 7 glossary keys, 15 short labels. Structural = placeholders/plurals/glossary/missing. Semantic = the checks only Layer 2 sees, chiefly the Spanish opening ¿.

8gb._measured_on: RTX 2070 Super, 8 GB, Ollama, 2026-07-27. CAVEAT on every wall time: the machine's RAM was later found running at 2133 MT/s — the JEDEC fallback, XMP never enabled (docs/HANDOFF.md, 2026-07-28). Models too big for 8 GB stream offloaded layers through exactly that RAM, so absolute times should improve at the rated 3600 and gaps like translategemma's 5x may shrink. Flag counts are unaffected; re-measure before leaning on any time below.

recommended.result: 0 structural failures across two runs; 1 and 2 semantic flags; 0/5 and 0/5 missing ¿; 219-227 s for the corpus
recommended.why: won a two-model bake-off scored mechanically. Both candidates were structurally perfect, so the winner is the one with fewer semantic flags — and the decisive one was the missing Spanish opening ¿, where qwen3:8b failed 1 and 5 times WITH the rule in its prompt. That is a model property, not a prompt problem.

alternatives.result: 0 structural failures; 2 semantic flags; 233 s — ONE corpus run (the winner has two)
alternatives.why: first-party Tencent GGUF from the translation-specialist Hy-MT2 family. Tied the winner's flag count in a single run at 57% of its disk size — but one run does not unseat a two-run winner, so a second run is the cheap way to settle this tier (queued in docs/HANDOFF.md).

alternatives.result: 0 structural failures; 3 and 7 semantic flags; missed the opening ¿ 1 and 5 times; 116-160 s
alternatives.why: the fast option, and the cautionary tale: it passes every structural check and is measurably the weakest on Spanish punctuation. Pick it only if wall time matters more than a review pass.

a purpose-built translation model, and it is genuinely clean. It is not the recommendation because it took 5x the winner's time on identical hardware for the same result. On a bigger card it may well be the best choice here.

avoid.result: 39/40 keys, translated the do-not-translate brand `Strands` to `Hilos`, lost a plural pipe
avoid.why: the specialised-model trap. Translation-tuned, and at 4B it lacks the instruction-following to honour a glossary — it faithfully translates the thing you told it not to. Its 12B sibling has no such problem, which is exactly why size-of-a-good-family is not evidence.

candidates.why: the flagship MoE — 26B with ~4B active, so it runs on an 8 GB card by streaming offloaded layers, and under the OLD wrapper pipeline it was the FASTEST local model measured (147 s for the corpus) with one identical-halves plural bug, exactly the class shielding now prevents by construction. NOT `measured` because that word means 'ran the corpus through THIS tool', and its run here was staged 2026-07-28 but died at startup — Ollama still held another model, and two engines cannot share 8 GB. Re-run queued after the XMP fix (docs/HANDOFF.md, 'THE RUN THAT WAS INTERRUPTED'); if the old-pipeline speed holds, it contends for the recommendation.

4gb_and_under._note: Nothing here is measured. The only small model tested at all, translategemma:4b, FAILED — so this tier has no recommendation rather than a guess. Candidates worth running: Hy-MT2-1.8B (first-party Tencent GGUF, reported to beat some commercial translation APIs) and gemma3:4b.

16gb._note: Untested — no 16 GB card here. The evidence-backed reasoning is that the two models measured clean at 8 GB (gemma3:12b, translategemma:12b) both fit comfortably and translategemma:12b's 5x time penalty should largely disappear once it stops offloading. That is a hypothesis, not a result.

candidates.why: first-party Tencent GGUF, 187k downloads on the base repo. A 30B MoE with ~3B active — the quality of a large model at the speed of a small one, which is the shape that makes MoE interesting on constrained hardware.
the largest TranslateGemma; its 12B sibling was measured clean.
larger sibling of the 8 GB winner.

24gb_plus._note: Untested. Listed so users with the hardware know where to look, explicitly NOT as recommendations.

candidates.why: the same MoE at a higher quant.
Unbabel's translation-specialist family at its largest. Note the GGUFs are third-party quants; the first-party release is safetensors.
small for this tier, but it won 30 of 31 language categories at WMT25 — worth measuring anywhere it fits.

cloud.result: 40/40, 0 structural, 0 semantic, 94 s — the best quality-per-second measured here
cloud.why: and unusable for real work: the free tier is 20 requests per DAY per model. One 846-key catalogue is 36 requests. Use it to prove a config, not to translate a product.
